tagline.text: A sea snake sanctuary and Malapascua's signature tunnel dive site

location.label: Location
location.text: Under Daanbantayan, Cebu, in the middle of the Visayan Sea northwest of Malapascua Island

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Year-round (January–June recommended, outside the rainy season)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Half day to 1 day (2-dive trip from Malapascua)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱3,600~6,000 (2 dives plus gear and environmental fees, departing from Malapascua)

children.text: Gato Island is a small rocky island about 1 hour by boat from Malapascua, and the waters around it are a sea snake and fish sanctuary. It is a signature dive where divers meet whitetip reef sharks, banded sea snakes and nudibranchs and swim through a shallow tunnel beneath the island.
Gato Island is a small rocky island rising in the middle of the Visayan Sea. It lies about
15km

northwest of Malapascua Island and belongs administratively to the municipality of Daanbantayan in Cebu. The name is Spanish for "Cat Island" (Isla del Gato), said to come from its resemblance to a curled, sleeping cat when seen from mainland Cebu. Its highest point is listed as about 83 m, though a 1919 survey recorded about 57 m, so sources differ.

The island is said to have become known in 1933, when two Japanese fishermen found a sea snake breeding ground there. In 1997 Daanbantayan declared the island a sea snake and fish sanctuary, and in 2001 the protected area was extended to 2 nautical miles around the island and placed under the municipal government. Many seabirds live on the island and some animals move in and out of its sea caves. It is also known as habitat of the yellow-lipped sea krait, which locals call "balingkasaw."

For travelers, Gato Island is a diving destination. The island itself is cut by waves and currents into cliffs and is almost impossible to dock at, so it is not a sightseeing stop for landing. What draws divers instead are the reef around it and its cave and tunnel formations. The best known is the tunnel that runs through the island (locally also called a cave), listed in guides at about 20–40 m long and shallow enough to be presented as a route that Open Water divers can attempt. Passing through usually takes about
30 minutes
, and reports say the entry is a narrow spot between boulders and under an overhang, so you may feel tense the first time.

Gato Island is often planned together with the thresher shark dives of Malapascua. Both depart from Malapascua, so you can simply ask your dive shop to arrange the schedule. There is not much to do for travelers who do not dive. Non-divers are said to be able to snorkel, but should be careful because of the sea snakes.
The highlight of diving at Gato Island is the tunnel beneath the island. The entrance begins at about
depth, and guides mention a line leading from the surface at the entrance. The length is given as about

depending on the guide, and the sandy floor does not stir up silt and the space is wide, so divers of several levels go in. A short stretch in the middle is said to receive no daylight, so bring a flashlight. The exit opens into a cathedral-like space on the far side of the island.
Whitetip reef sharks can be seen resting or circling inside the tunnel, at its entrance and at sites such as "Whitetip Alley." Adults are said to grow to about
2m
in length. Many sharks rest during the day, so moving less lets you watch them longer. Rays circling at the "Cathedral" formation are also reported.

The whole island is a sea snake sanctuary, so divers say banded sea snakes are almost guaranteed. They are venomous but known to be docile. Even so, do not touch them or chase them, and keep your distance. Small seahorses are also said to live among the coral heads and rocks near the large cave entrance.

"Nudibranch City" around the island is said to have many kinds of nudibranchs in one place. Macro life such as banded boxer shrimp, seahorses and frogfish has been reported, along with a Spanish dancer about
30cm
long. It is popular with divers who enjoy macro photography.
At the Guardhouse site, at about
depth, a dwarf seahorse can reportedly be seen. It is deeper than the tunnel, so follow your guide and stay within your certification and experience.

On the side of the island there is a small cave opening that boats can enter. At high tide the opening is small and it is hard to maneuver a boat. The coastline is a cliff cut by waves, so docking is almost impossible, and with strong currents boats approach the rock face only with great care.

blocks.title: Small life in the tunnel and on the reef

children.text: Divers report Tubastrea corals and sponges on the tunnel walls, with shrimps, spider crabs, hermit crabs and a large sponge crab. Lionfish, a moray eel, squirrelfish, a school of striped catfish and the tail of a bamboo shark have also been seen. On the reef on the far side of the tunnel, seahorses, pipefish, scorpionfish, sea snakes, pufferfish, a school of mackerel, nudibranchs and two cuttlefish have been recorded. What you see differs every day, so keep your expectations open.

items.title: One-day dive trip
items.subtitle: Two dives at Gato Island from Malapascua

children.text: Collect your gear at the dive shop and attend the briefing. Departure times differ by shop, so confirm them the day before.
Board the bangka and head for Gato Island. It takes about
50 minutes to 1 hour
from Malapascua.
On the first dive, swim through the tunnel and explore the reef on the far side. Reports say the tunnel section lasts about
30 minutes
After a surface interval, make a second dive. Sites such as Nudibranch City or Whitetip Alley are candidates.
Have lunch and return to Malapascua.
Rinse and dry your gear and log your dives. Spend the afternoon relaxing on the beach as part of your surface time.
The order can change with currents and waves, so follow the dive master's judgment for the final plan.

items.title: 2–3 days in Malapascua
items.subtitle: Thresher sharks and Gato Island together

children.text: Make an early-morning thresher shark dive at Monad Shoal (see the Malapascua entry for details).
Rest or relax on the beach.
Make two dives at Gato Island.
Keep any remaining days for nearby sites or as spare days.
Schedule flights or ferries for at least about
18–24 hours
after your last dive, which is the general safety recommendation.
Fly from Manila Ninoy Aquino Airport to Mactan-Cebu Airport (CEB), which takes about
1 hour 20 minutes
The usual route is a bus from the Cebu north bus terminal to Maya port in Daanbantayan. Travel times and fares vary by season, so check at the terminal.

items.title: From Cebu to Maya port and Malapascua

children.text: Travel by bus or van from Cebu City to Maya port in northern Daanbantayan, then take a public boat from Maya to Malapascua. Check boat times and fares locally.
Most divers stay on Malapascua and go to Gato Island through a dive shop.
A dive shop bangka takes about
50 minutes to 1 hour
from Malapascua to Gato Island. The trip is normally a 2-dive outing.
The island is also said to be reachable from the Daanbantayan barangays of Tapilon, Maya and Logon. Travelers usually go through a dive shop.
There is no landing facility on the island. Boats wait close to the rock face.
Sharks and sea snakes at Gato Island are said to be seen all year. Diving is possible year-round too, but the sea is relatively stable in
January–June
, outside the rainy season. Water temperature ranges from about
July–December
is the rainy season in this area. Gato Island is close to open water, so waves and currents can be strong and visibility can drop, so keep spare days.

Most divers stay on Malapascua in a resort that has a dive shop. There is no lodging on Gato Island, so you visit from Malapascua. Packages that combine lodging and diving are common, so ask the shop and compare room rates as well.

Meals are taken at resort restaurants and beach stalls on Malapascua. Some dive tours include lunch, so check the shop's description. Bring your own water and snacks. Gato Island trips normally dive twice and return to Malapascua, so ask in advance whether the shop provides lunch or you eat at the island. Simple meals of grilled seafood, rice and noodles are common on Malapascua.
Guides say Open Water divers can enter the Gato Island tunnel, but shops may require 10–20 logged dives or more. Ask about the experience requirement first.
In the tunnel, keep your buoyancy stable and fin slowly so you do not stir up the sandy floor. If visibility drops, the divers behind you are at risk.
Do not approach sharks that are resting. Pass slowly in single file, since the less you move, the longer you can watch them.
A flashlight is essential. You can also rent one from the shop.
Do not touch or chase sea snakes. They are said to be docile despite their venom, but the rule is not to provoke them.
When using an underwater camera, avoid startling nocturnal creatures with your flash.
If you worry about seasickness, take medication before departure. The trip to Gato Island crosses open water.
Do not go up to high places or board a plane right after diving. Leave some slack on your last day.
Do not put your hands on coral or the rock walls, and practice neutral buoyancy beforehand to make the tunnel much easier.
Dive with a guide suited to your certification and experience. Currents at Gato Island are strong and waves at the entrance can be rough, and you must also observe the no-fly time before a flight.
The island is a sanctuary. Do not collect or touch living things such as corals, sea snakes or shells.
In the July–December rainy season, trips can be canceled because of waves and currents.
The cliffs around the island are sharp and boats find it hard to dock. The guide decides safe spots for snorkeling.
Cost information differs between sources and includes outdated figures. Get a current quote from the shop.
The tunnel has narrow stretches, so tell your guide in advance if you have claustrophobia.
